title: The oxygen crossing
q: In a lung with the usual gas-pressure gradients, where does oxygen move from an alveolus?
explanation: Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into the adjacent pulmonary capillary blood, driven by a partial-pressure difference. The figure shows the net direction, not individual molecular paths.

title: The other gas crossing
q: At the lung, where does carbon dioxide move from pulmonary capillary blood under the usual gradient?
explanation: Carbon dioxide diffuses from pulmonary capillary blood into alveolar air under the usual partial-pressure gradient. It can then leave the body in exhaled air.

title: A plant's water route
q: In a transpiring plant, water absorbed by roots travels through xylem toward which structure?
explanation: Water absorbed by roots moves through xylem toward leaves. Transpiration at the leaf helps pull water along this route; the drawing omits the branching vessels.

title: A plant's sugar route
q: A mature leaf is a sugar source and a growing root is a sugar sink. Through phloem, where can sugar move?
explanation: Phloem transports sugars from sources to sinks. In this example the mature leaf supplies a growing root; source and sink roles can change with development.

title: Water leaves the leaf
q: During transpiration, where does water vapour leave a leaf through open stomata?
explanation: Transpiration transfers water vapour from the leaf to the atmosphere, largely through stomata. Evaporation and the water-vapour gradient drive this loss.

title: The kidney's first filter
q: A kidney glomerulus filters blood. Where does the initial filtrate collect before entering the tubule?
explanation: Fluid filtered from glomerular capillaries enters Bowman's capsule before passing into the tubule. Blood cells and most large proteins normally remain in the blood.

title: A return trip in the kidney
q: During renal tubular reabsorption, where does a recovered solute go from the tubule fluid?
explanation: Reabsorption moves selected substances from the nephron tubule back toward the circulation through surrounding capillaries. The diagram omits the intermediate tissue fluid.

title: A message crosses the gap
q: At a chemical synapse, a released neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic cleft. What can it bind on the receiving cell?
explanation: A neurotransmitter released by the sending neuron can cross the cleft and bind receptors on the receiving cell. The response depends on the receptor and cell.

title: A long-distance signal
q: A hormone released by an endocrine cell reaches a distant target. Which transport route commonly carries it there?
explanation: Endocrine hormones travel through the bloodstream to distant tissues. A target cell responds when it has an appropriate receptor; not every cell responds to every hormone.

title: A pollen delivery
q: In a flowering plant, pollination places pollen from an anther onto which receptive flower structure?
explanation: In flowering plants, pollination is pollen transfer from an anther to a stigma. Pollination is a step before fertilization, not the fusion of sperm and egg itself.

title: Two gametes meet
q: When a sperm cell fuses with an egg cell in fertilization, what single cell results?
explanation: Fertilization combines sperm and egg to form a zygote. The figure represents the fusion step, not the many later divisions of the developing organism.

title: A seed starts growing
q: A viable seed has water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. When germination succeeds, what begins to emerge and grow?
explanation: With suitable conditions, a viable seed can germinate and the embryo resumes growth into a seedling. Requirements vary across species, so water, oxygen and temperature are not a complete rule for every seed.

title: Nitrogen enters a living route
q: Certain nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into which form?
explanation: Nitrogen-fixing microorganisms convert N₂ into ammonia, which can become ammonium in water. The diagram summarizes the conversion and omits its enzyme and energy requirements.

title: First nitrification step
q: In a common two-step nitrification pathway, microorganisms oxidize ammonium first to which nitrogen compound?
explanation: In a common nitrification pathway, ammonium is oxidized to nitrite; another step can oxidize nitrite to nitrate. The model shows the first conversion only.

title: Second nitrification step
q: In a common nitrification pathway, microorganisms can oxidize nitrite into which compound?
explanation: In a common nitrification pathway, nitrite is oxidized to nitrate. This is the second conversion after ammonium is oxidized to nitrite.

title: Nitrogen returns to the air
q: During denitrification, certain microorganisms can convert nitrate into which form that returns to the atmosphere?
explanation: Denitrifying microorganisms can convert nitrate through several intermediate forms to nitrogen gas. The simplified arrow summarizes the pathway rather than showing every intermediate.

title: Carbon enters a plant
q: In photosynthesis, carbon from atmospheric carbon dioxide can become part of which product?
explanation: Photosynthesis incorporates carbon from carbon dioxide into organic molecules such as sugars. Light energy and water are also involved; the diagram follows the carbon, not every input and output.

title: Carbon leaves a fuel
q: During aerobic cellular respiration, carbon atoms from glucose can leave a cell in which product?
explanation: Aerobic cellular respiration breaks down glucose and releases its carbon as carbon dioxide. Oxygen is consumed and water and ATP are also produced; the picture tracks carbon only.

title: Breaking down protein
q: After protein digestion is completed, which small building blocks can be absorbed from the intestine?
explanation: Digestive enzymes break proteins into smaller peptides and amino acids; amino acids can be absorbed by the intestine. The arrow summarizes multiple enzyme steps.

title: Breaking down starch
q: After the complete digestion of starch, which monosaccharide can be absorbed?
explanation: Starch is broken into smaller carbohydrates and ultimately glucose by digestive enzymes. The arrow summarizes the sequence rather than showing every intermediate.

title: Breaking down dietary fat
q: Pancreatic lipase acts on a triglyceride. Which products are typical of its initial digestion?
explanation: Pancreatic lipase typically releases two fatty acids from a triglyceride, leaving a monoglyceride. MG labels monoglyceride; the schematic omits emulsification and absorption.
